args.summary: 32F with meningomyelocele, radical cystectomy for bladder cancer and a continent MAINZ pouch I diversion. She had weeks of increasing difficulty catheterizing, and an indwelling pouch catheter was placed. That catheter stopped draining last night and urine output fell. She now has severe lower abdominal pain, dyspnea and cardiopulmonary decompensation. Urgent CT with retrograde pouch contrast shows a large left laterodorsal reservoir defect with contrast leaking into the peritoneum and free intraperitoneal fluid. This fits spontaneous rupture of an obstructed, overdistended continent pouch causing urinary peritonitis, possibly with early sepsis or urinary ascites limiting diaphragm movement.
working_diagnoses: Spontaneous rupture of MAINZ pouch I continent urinary reservoir with intraperitoneal urine leak (urinary peritonitis)
Acute kidney injury / pseudo-renal failure from peritoneal urine reabsorption
Respiratory compromise from abdominal distension/urinary ascites with possible aspiration or PE
Pouch/stoma outlet obstruction (stomal stenosis, mucus or stone) as the precipitant
next_actions: Stat labs: CBC, chemistry/creatinine/electrolytes, lactate, inflammatory markers, coagulation
Blood and urine/pouch cultures, then IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
IV fluid resuscitation and oxygen, with hemodynamic monitoring
Decompress the pouch (catheter re-placement) and arrange emergent laparotomy to repair the pouch defect and lavage the peritoneum

facts.value: Before surgery: WBC 15.3×10^9/L, hemoglobin 143 g/L, platelets 513×10^9/L.
Before surgery: sodium 138 mmol/L, creatinine 1.08 mg/dL, eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m².

args.rationale: Emergency laparotomy confirmed a spontaneous rupture of the MAINZ pouch I, which was repaired. The pouch catheter was fixed in place and an NG tube was placed. She came in with cardiopulmonary decompensation and urinary peritonitis. WBC was 15.3 before surgery. Postoperative vital signs and a chest X-ray were not available, and pulmonary embolism has not been excluded. She needs continuous monitoring.
args.followup_or_handoff: ICU handoff: monitor hemodynamics and breathing; give supplemental oxygen or ventilatory support as needed; manage fluids with strict intake and output. Continue IV piperacillin-tazobactam but confirm there is no beta-lactam allergy first; send pouch urine, blood and peritoneal cultures and adjust antibiotics to the results. Keep the pouch catheter draining continuously and flush it regularly to clear mucus; do not clamp it. Keep the NG tube on decompression. Order serial lactate, CBC, CRP, creatinine and electrolytes. Get a chest X-ray and ECG. Consider CTPA if dyspnea continues. Give VTE prophylaxis. Urology should review daily. Before removing the catheter, do a pouchogram to confirm the repair has healed. Once recovered, investigate the cause of the difficult catheterization (stomal or outlet stenosis, stones, mucus) and plan a definitive fix.
